currentContext.strengths: World's largest joint-replacement centre by volume (175,000+ surgeries performed, ranked first globally in arthroplasty by volume), built on founder Dr. Vikram Shah's proprietary 'zero technique' for knee replacement|Integrated ecosystem model: hospitals, implant manufacturing (California) and the international patient business share clinical knowledge, brand and technology — hospitals give the implant business a demanding home market and clinical feedback, while the implant business gives hospitals supply security and cost control|Speciality diversification away from single-procedure dependence: arthroplasty, once the overwhelming majority of clinical revenue, is now roughly a third of it, with oncology, cardiac sciences, critical care, nephrology and transplants filling the balance|Capital-efficient expansion via franchise-owned/Shalby-managed and revenue-sharing operating models (e.g. Zynova Mumbai, Gwalior, Vijay Ahmedabad units), extending the brand into new markets with limited capital|International patient brand draws patients from more than 60 countries across a care presence in 23 international markets and 60 domestic OPD clinics|Early adopter of advanced clinical technology — including the world's first fully autonomous robotic joint replacement, robotic systems across urology, oncology, gynaecology and orthopaedics, PET-CT and radiotherapy — supporting premium clinical positioning|In-house academy and training initiatives to address the clinical workforce shortage, aiding talent attraction and retention
currentContext.strategies: Raise occupancy on existing beds and deepen the speciality case mix in the hospital business, improving return on capital through operating discipline rather than heavy new capital spending|Keep the medical-technology (US knee/hip implant) business growing while managing the working capital it consumes|Bring the planned Mumbai facility (Asha Parekh Hospital) forward on schedule to extend the group's reach into the Mumbai healthcare market|Narrow the operating loss at Shalby International (the Delhi-NCR/Gurugram international-patient business) as it builds scale|Expand implant distribution into international markets and pursue robotic-implant launches abroad, while equipping Shalby's own theatres with implants controlled from design to delivery|Grow Shalby Academy's training programmes to build the allied-health workforce (nursing, physiotherapy, lab and OT technicians) that all three businesses depend on|Expand 24x7 homecare services, supported by digital systems, to extend care beyond hospital walls and enter new service markets|Evolve the hospital business towards a preferred Operations & Management (O&M) partner model as part of capital-efficient, franchise-based expansion|Continue diversifying the clinical portfolio beyond arthroplasty into cardiac sciences, oncology, neurosciences, critical care, nephrology, gastroenterology, urology and transplants|The Board of Directors did not recommend a dividend for FY2025-26. The Company maintains a Dividend Distribution Policy (in line with SEBI LODR Regulation 43A) setting out the circumstances, financial parameters and internal/external factors governing whether members may expect a dividend. The Board did not transfer any amount out of profit to General Reserves for the year, choosing instead to retain the entire profit in the Profit and Loss account.
currentContext.expansion: Growth is planned as selective, profitability-led greenfield and brownfield hospital additions layered on an asset-light franchise/management model, rather than broad-based bed addition. The named upcoming project is the planned Mumbai (Santacruz) hospital. During the year the Company raised its stake in the Gurugram international hospital (PK Healthcare) to over 91% via a rights issue and secured NABH accreditation for that unit; commissioned oncology departments with advanced radiotherapy at the Krishna (Ahmedabad) and Surat units; installed PET-CT and radiotherapy capability across three units; obtained a five-year kidney-transplant approval for the Krishna unit; performed the world's first fully autonomous robotic joint-replacement surgery and commissioned robotic surgical systems at two centres; and closed two EBITDA-negative units, reallocating capital towards higher-return opportunities including the now EBITDA-positive Shalby MedTech implant business, which is being scaled across domestic and export markets with planned new product launches.
currentContext.mdna: India remains structurally under-bedded (about 1.3 hospital beds per 1,000 people versus a much higher global median), a long-run capacity opportunity for organised players|Steady migration of patients from unorganised to organised, accredited healthcare providers|Deepening penetration of organised care into Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities|Industry-wide shift towards asset-light, capital-efficient hospital expansion (franchise/managed models), which the Company is positioned to participate in|Consolidation among corporate hospital chains is raising the importance of scale, clinical depth and brand|Deepening health-insurance penetration is expanding the pool of patients able to access organised, quality care|India's medical-device and orthopaedic-implant market remains heavily import-dependent (roughly 70-80% of demand met by imports), and government policy (Make in India, PLI scheme, customs-duty relief on implant inputs) is creating an opening for credible domestic/integrated manufacturers such as the Company's implant business|Ageing population and the rising burden of non-communicable diseases (cardiac, cancer, diabetes, degenerative joint disorders) are driving demand across orthopaedics, cardiac sciences, oncology and nephrology|Medical tourism/medical-value-travel to India continues to grow, though the West Asia conflict disrupted patient flows from parts of the Middle East during the year, partly offset by inflows from Africa and the CIS region|Global healthcare shifts relevant to the Company: migration of value towards medical technology and devices, broadening of clinical portfolios by leading providers, and a consumer shift towards organised, accredited, technology-enabled care

risks.note: The West Asia conflict reduced patient inflows from parts of the Middle East during the year; the international business's source-market mix (partly offset by Africa/CIS inflows) leaves it exposed to further geopolitical disruption. Mitigated by diversifying source markets and leveraging the Gurugram unit's new NABH accreditation to broaden referrals.

risks.risk: Input-cost and currency risk on imported devices/consumables
risks.note: Imported medical devices and consumables expose the Company to currency and input-cost volatility; mitigated structurally through in-house implant manufacturing (vertical integration) and a natural hedge from Shalby MedTech's export revenues.

risks.risk: Margin and new-specialty ramp-up / execution risk
risks.note: New specialties, new units and the international/MedTech businesses take time to reach maturity and breakeven, which can compress margins; managed via a phased, profitability-led roll-out, close unit-level economics monitoring, and willingness to exit underperforming units (two loss-making units closed during the year).

Price controls on devices and procedures, evolving device regulation, and government-scheme reimbursement rates can affect realisations; mitigated through strong clinical governance, accreditation, compliance and active engagement with the regulatory framework.

A persistent shortage of doctors, nurses and allied-health professionals could constrain capacity and raise wage costs; mitigated through investment in Shalby Academy, training pipelines and clinician engagement/retention initiatives.

Group leverage (net debt/equity of about 0.44x) is concentrated in the medical-technology and international businesses rather than the hospitals; mitigated by conservative gearing, MedTech's move to EBITDA breakeven reducing further funding needs, and an unencumbered promoter holding.

As a healthcare provider, the Company's brand and patient trust depend on maintaining stringent quality protocols, accreditation and patient-safety systems; any lapse could materially affect its clinical brand and referral base.

Growing reliance on IT systems and clinical-information systems across the hospital network creates data-protection and cybersecurity exposure; mitigated through continued investment in IT systems and data-protection controls.

one-line thesis: Shalby delivered a sharp Q4 profitability inflection driven by a structural tax rate reduction (35% to 25%) and Shalby MedTech's first sustained EBITDA positivity, offsetting single-digit hospital revenue growth hampered by geopolitical headwinds in international patient inflows. The narrative shifts from pure capacity addition to operating leverage realization, with FY27 poised for margin expansion as heavy oncology/robotics capex moderates and new surgeon hires mature.
financial scorecard: Revenue: INR 295.5cr (+9.4% YoY); EBITDA: INR 37.4cr (+43.1% YoY), Margin 12.7% (vs 9.7%); PAT: INR 18.5cr (vs Loss INR 12.2cr) - Major one-off/structural benefit from tax regime change; Net Debt: INR 446.2cr (Gearing 0.44x); Order Book: N/A (Service/Inventory model).
guidance: Revenue Growth: Min 15% CAGR long-term for hospitals; MedTech target INR 600-700cr by 2030; Margins: MedTech targeting >15% EBITDA by 2030, Hospital margins to expand post-doctor stabilization; Capex: Significant spend in FY26 (INR 160cr), expected to moderate in FY27.
order book & pipeline: N/A for hospital services; MedTech focusing on inventory turnover improvement and demand-driven planning rather than traditional order book; Pipeline includes regulatory approvals in Vietnam, Malaysia, Myanmar.
segment / subsidiary detail: Hospitals: Rev INR 295.5cr (Consol), Occupancy 48% (50% ex-Gurugram), ARPOB INR 42,689 (+2.7%); MedTech: Rev INR 40cr (Q4, +45% YoY), EBITDA INR 3.7cr (2nd consecutive positive quarter); International (Gurugram): Rev INR 21.5cr (-5.7% YoY) due to Middle East conflict, 47% revenue from intl patients.
growth verticals / optionality: MedTech scale-up to INR 600cr+ by 2030 with robotics (Curexo partnership); Oncology expansion via new LINAC bunkers (Surat, Krishna) driving high-value cases; International patient diversification into CIS/Africa to offset Middle East volatility.
margins & cost dynamics: Gross margin dipped to ~85% (from 90%) due to new doctor onboarding costs and expensive oncology medicines; EBITDA margin expanded to 12.7% primarily due to tax rate shift (25% vs 35%) and MedTech operating leverage; Doctor attrition in Q2/Q3 resolved, stability expected to restore margins in Q2FY27.
capex / expansion: FY26 Capex ~INR 160cr focused on Oncology (LINAC bunkers in Surat/Krishna) and Robotics; FY27 capex expected to be minimal as major infrastructure investments are complete, aiding free cash flow.
capital allocation: Debt reduction prioritized post-MedTech breakeven; Equity infusion of INR 60cr in Shalby International (Gurugram) to strengthen balance sheet (stake increased to 91%); Franchisee model de-prioritized in favor of core owned assets.
risks & watch-items: Geopolitical tension (US-Iran/Middle East) suppressing high-margin international patient inflows; Doctor attrition turbulence impacting short-term utilization; Government scheme payment delays; Execution risk in MedTech global expansion.
management quality / tone: Cautiously optimistic; Emphasizes 'inflection point' for MedTech profitability; Confident on margin recovery post-doctor stabilization; Transparent about geopolitical headwinds but highlights successful diversification to CIS/Africa.
non-obvious takeaways: The gross margin compression is a temporary function of oncology mix (high drug cost) and new doctor ramp-up, not structural deterioration; Franchisee model is being quietly deprioritized due to quality control issues, shifting focus entirely to owned assets and MedTech; Tax benefit is recurring, not a one-time gain, fundamentally resetting the PAT baseline.

themes.title: Hospitals, diagnostics & domestic healthcare
themes.need: Under-bedded India plus insurance penetration and preventive-care adoption drive a domestic healthcare capex + volume cycle distinct from export pharma. MAXHEALTH adding ~2,500+ beds (Gurgaon 500-bed by FY27); APOLLOHOSP/MEDANTA/KIMS/NH/ASTERDM/MAXHEALTH on hospitals; LALPATHLAB/METROPOLIS/THYROCARE/VIJAYA on diagnostics (LALPATHLAB guides 13-15% FY27); MEDPLUS/ENTERO on pharmacy/distribution; POLYMED on devices. The same India-only demand engine now also carries India-facing branded pharma, which is driven by domestic volume and price rather than the export book: GLAXO delivered its first INR 1,000cr quarter with 8.1% revenue growth, Shingrix at a ~INR 75cr annual run-rate (CY25, +80% YoY) and Jemperli's first-line approval expanding eligible patients from 800 to 6,000; ERIS (dermatology 15% of revenue after INR 1,265cr of domestic brand acquisitions), SANOFI (India-for-India, NLEM price cuts) and THEMISMED (hospital segment +20% YoY) sit on the same axis.
themes.driver: New-bed commissioning + occupancy ramp; Tier 3/4 diagnostics penetration; CGHS rate revision; preventive-test volumes; domestic branded-formulation volume growth and NLEM/price actions.

hero.oneLiner: Shalby Limited is one of India's leading speciality hospital groups and, by volume, the world's largest joint-replacement centre, now extending into an integrated ecosystem of hospitals, medical-technology (implant) manufacturing and international patient care.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Shalby Limited is one of India's leading speciality hospital groups and, by volume, the world's largest joint-replacement centre, now extending into an integrated ecosystem of hospitals, medical-technology (implant) manufacturing and international patient care.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Shalby operates a network of 13 multi- and single-speciality hospitals (2,200+ beds) across western, central and northern India, anchored in orthopaedics/arthroplasty and now spanning cardiac sciences, oncology, neurosciences, critical care, nephrology, gastroenterology, urology and organ transplantation. It also runs an orthopaedic implant (knee and hip) manufacturing business in California, United States, an international patient business serving patients from 60+ countries, a home-care division, and an academy for allied-health training, with the businesses sharing clinical knowledge, brand and technology.

guidance.title: Guidance
guidance.body: Revenue Growth: Min 15% CAGR long-term for hospitals; MedTech target INR 600-700cr by 2030; Margins: MedTech targeting >15% EBITDA by 2030, Hospital margins to expand post-doctor stabilization; Capex: Significant spend in FY26 (INR 160cr), expected to moderate in FY27.

growth_optionality.title: Growth verticals / optionality
growth_optionality.body: MedTech scale-up to INR 600cr+ by 2030 with robotics (Curexo partnership); Oncology expansion via new LINAC bunkers (Surat, Krishna) driving high-value cases; International patient diversification into CIS/Africa to offset Middle East volatility.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India remains structurally under-bedded (about 1.3 hospital beds per 1,000 people versus a much higher global median), a long-run capacity opportunity for organised players
- Steady migration of patients from unorganised to organised, accredited healthcare providers
- Deepening penetration of organised care into Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities
- Industry-wide shift towards asset-light, capital-efficient hospital expansion (franchise/managed models), which the Company is positioned to participate in
- Consolidation among corporate hospital chains is raising the importance of scale, clinical depth and brand
- Deepening health-insurance penetration is expanding the pool of patients able to access organised, quality care
- India's medical-device and orthopaedic-implant market remains heavily import-dependent (roughly 70-80% of demand met by imports), and government policy (Make in India, PLI scheme, customs-duty relief on implant inputs) is creating an opening for credible domestic/integrated manufacturers such as the Company's implant business
- Ageing population and the rising burden of non-communicable diseases (cardiac, cancer, diabetes, degenerative joint disorders) are driving demand across orthopaedics, cardiac sciences, oncology and nephrology
- Medical tourism/medical-value-travel to India continues to grow, though the West Asia conflict disrupted patient flows from parts of the Middle East during the year, partly offset by inflows from Africa and the CIS region
- Global healthcare shifts relevant to the Company: migration of value towards medical technology and devices, broadening of clinical portfolios by leading providers, and a consumer shift towards organised, accredited, technology-enabled care

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: Gross margin dipped to ~85% (from 90%) due to new doctor onboarding costs and expensive oncology medicines; EBITDA margin expanded to 12.7% primarily due to tax rate shift (25% vs 35%) and MedTech operating leverage; Doctor attrition in Q2/Q3 resolved, stability expected to restore margins in Q2FY27.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: Debt reduction prioritized post-MedTech breakeven; Equity infusion of INR 60cr in Shalby International (Gurugram) to strengthen balance sheet (stake increased to 91%); Franchisee model de-prioritized in favor of core owned assets.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Growth is planned as selective, profitability-led greenfield and brownfield hospital additions layered on an asset-light franchise/management model, rather than broad-based bed addition. The named upcoming project is the planned Mumbai (Santacruz) hospital. During the year the Company raised its stake in the Gurugram international hospital (PK Healthcare) to over 91% via a rights issue and secured NABH accreditation for that unit; commissioned oncology departments with advanced radiotherapy at the Krishna (Ahmedabad) and Surat units; installed PET-CT and radiotherapy capability across three units; obtained a five-year kidney-transplant approval for the Krishna unit; performed the world's first fully autonomous robotic joint-replacement surgery and commissioned robotic surgical systems at two centres; and closed two EBITDA-negative units, reallocating capital towards higher-return opportunities including the now EBITDA-positive Shalby MedTech implant business, which is being scaled across domestic and export markets with planned new product launches.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Cautiously optimistic; Emphasizes 'inflection point' for MedTech profitability; Confident on margin recovery post-doctor stabilization; Transparent about geopolitical headwinds but highlights successful diversification to CIS/Africa.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- World's largest joint-replacement centre by volume (175,000+ surgeries performed, ranked first globally in arthroplasty by volume), built on founder Dr. Vikram Shah's proprietary 'zero technique' for knee replacement
- Integrated ecosystem model: hospitals, implant manufacturing (California) and the international patient business share clinical knowledge, brand and technology — hospitals give the implant business a demanding home market and clinical feedback, while the implant business gives hospitals supply security and cost control
- Speciality diversification away from single-procedure dependence: arthroplasty, once the overwhelming majority of clinical revenue, is now roughly a third of it, with oncology, cardiac sciences, critical care, nephrology and transplants filling the balance
- Capital-efficient expansion via franchise-owned/Shalby-managed and revenue-sharing operating models (e.g. Zynova Mumbai, Gwalior, Vijay Ahmedabad units), extending the brand into new markets with limited capital
- International patient brand draws patients from more than 60 countries across a care presence in 23 international markets and 60 domestic OPD clinics
- Early adopter of advanced clinical technology — including the world's first fully autonomous robotic joint replacement, robotic systems across urology, oncology, gynaecology and orthopaedics, PET-CT and radiotherapy — supporting premium clinical positioning
- In-house academy and training initiatives to address the clinical workforce shortage, aiding talent attraction and retention

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: Geopolitical tension (US-Iran/Middle East) suppressing high-margin international patient inflows; Doctor attrition turbulence impacting short-term utilization; Government scheme payment delays; Execution risk in MedTech global expansion.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: The gross margin compression is a temporary function of oncology mix (high drug cost) and new doctor ramp-up, not structural deterioration; Franchisee model is being quietly deprioritized due to quality control issues, shifting focus entirely to owned assets and MedTech; Tax benefit is recurring, not a one-time gain, fundamentally resetting the PAT baseline.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Raise occupancy on existing beds and deepen the speciality case mix in the hospital business, improving return on capital through operating discipline rather than heavy new capital spending
- Keep the medical-technology (US knee/hip implant) business growing while managing the working capital it consumes
- Bring the planned Mumbai facility (Asha Parekh Hospital) forward on schedule to extend the group's reach into the Mumbai healthcare market
- Narrow the operating loss at Shalby International (the Delhi-NCR/Gurugram international-patient business) as it builds scale
- Expand implant distribution …

challenges.title: Challenges → beneficiaries & losers
challenges.body:
| Challenge | Beneficiary/Loser | Dir | Conviction | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Global competitors facing higher manufacturing costs and slower innovation cycles in orthopedics. | Shalby Limited | beneficiary | High | MedTech division achieved consecutive positive EBITDA quarters with a clear path to 15%+ margins by 2030, validating the 'Designed in India' cost-arbitrage and innovation model. |
| Hospitals reliant on Middle Eastern medical tourism facing sustained patient inflow drops due to conflict. | Competitors with high GCC exposure | loser | Med | Shalby's Gurugram unit faced headwinds but successfully pivoted to CIS/African markets, whereas peers without this diversification may suffer prolonged revenue stagnation. |

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:
- [Shareholding] As on 30th June'26: Promoters 74.33%, Public 20.26%, FIIs 4.47%, Employee Benefit Trust 0.65%, DIIs 0.30%.
- [Group structure] Implant business sits under Shalby MedTech Limited (SMTL), "formerly known as Mars Medical Devices Limited (MMDL)", which holds Shalby Advanced Technologies Inc. (SAT), Shalby Global Technologies Pte Ltd (SGT) and Shalby Advanced Technologies (India) Pvt. Ltd.
- [MedTech scale-up] SMTL Consolidated total revenue was INR 584.41 mn in FY24, 922.86 mn in FY25 and 1,349.72 mn in FY26 (+46% YoY as labelled), with Total EBITDA of (48.52), (191.65) and 67.04 mn respectively - i.e. the implant arm turned EBITDA-positive at the FY26 level.
- [Long-term group trend] Consolidated Total Revenue (INR Crs) FY21 to FY26: 440, 711, 827, 953, 1115, 1168; EBITDA (INR Crs): 95, 132, 159, 196, 160, 170 with margins 22%, 19%, 19%, 21%, 14%, 15%. The slide prints two "5 years CAGR" figures (21.6% and 12.3%) that cannot be bound to their respective series from the extract, so neither CAGR is attributed here.
- [Governance] Board comprises Dr Vikram Shah (Chairman and Managing Director) plus five Independent Directors: Dr Ashok Bhatia, Mr Shyamal Joshi, Mr Tej Malhotra, Dr Umesh Menon and Ms Sujana Shah.
